title: Jeremiah on Trial
sum: Early in Jehoiakim's reign, Jeremiah stands in the Temple court and warns that if Judah will not listen, the LORD will make his house like Shiloh and the city a byword for cursing. The priests and prophets seize him and demand death. The royal officials come up from the palace and sit as judges at the New Gate. Jeremiah says only that the LORD sent him, that the people should mend their ways, and that killing him would bring innocent blood on the city.

The officials acquit him. Some elders then recall Micah of Moresheth, who said almost the same thing under Hezekiah and was not killed; the king listened and the harm did not come. The chapter ends with a darker story: Uriah, who prophesied the same message, was hunted down in Egypt and executed by Jehoiakim. Jeremiah lived only because the family of Shaphan protected him.
readings: The chapter is a short court case: charge (26:8–9), accusers (26:11), defense (26:12–15), verdict (26:16) and precedent (26:17–19). It shows that Judah had a legal tradition that protected prophets (Deuteronomy 18; Micah's case), though the king could bypass it (Uriah).
Read as the cost of the Temple sermon
Chapter 7 gives the words and chapter 26 the price. The reader meets the sermon twice, first as challenge and then as danger to the man who said it.

views.H: Dated to 609/608 BC. Josiah was dead, Necho had put Jehoiakim on the throne (2 Kings 23:34), and the Temple's priests and prophets trusted that Zion could not fall. The elders' appeal to Micah (Micah 3:12; Hezekiah's reign about 715–686 BC) is the one case in the prophets of a past prophecy cited as precedent, and Uriah's death shows the risk. Elnathan son of Achbor, who brings Uriah back, may be the Elnathan who later urges Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's scroll (36:25); the text does not say they are one man.
views.C: Most critics assign the chapter to the biographical prose (Mowinckel's source B, often credited to Baruch) and read it as the narrative frame for the Temple sermon of chapter 7, whose Deuteronomic style (source C) differs. The Greek calls the opponents "false prophets" throughout, and lacks "Elnathan son of Achbor" in 26:22 (see the variants). The Ketiv in 26:18 spells Micah as "Micaiah".
views.J: Jewish readers can point to the elders' use of Micah as the first case in Scripture of a prophet's words quoted as precedent. Deuteronomy 18:20 made death the penalty for a prophet who presumed to speak for God, and the priests apply it here; Jeremiah's defense is the Bible's example of a prophet answering that charge. Jewish tradition also names Jeremiah as the author of Lamentations (Bavli Bava Batra 15a).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Jeremiah a type of Christ, accused by the priests of speaking against the Temple (Matthew 26:61; Mark 14:58; Acts 6:13–14), and saved here, unlike Jesus. Jesus' own words about the Temple as a "den of robbers" (Matthew 21:13) echo Jeremiah 7:11, "a cave for bandits". Early writers such as Origen, in his homilies on Jeremiah, read Jeremiah's sufferings as a pattern for Christ and for the believer.
views.F: No future event is tied to this chapter.

deep.b: Shiloh was the home of the ark in the days of Eli and Samuel (1 Samuel 1–4). When the Philistines captured the ark and, it seems, destroyed the shrine, Israel's worship moved, and Psalm 78:60 says the LORD abandoned it. For Jeremiah's hearers Shiloh was ancient history; for him it was a warning that a holy place has no power on its own. Excavators (the Danish expedition, and Israel Finkelstein's from 1981) have reported a destruction layer at Tel Shiloh from about 1050 BC; the cause is debated, and the site was lived in thinly in later periods. Chapter 7 says the same thing at the Temple gate, and in chapter 26 the priests heard it as a death sentence for the Temple and, with it, for their own livelihood.

deep.h: A prophet's life depends on a court
deep.b: The story shows several ways a prophet was protected or endangered. The officials, who are royal appointees, judge on the basis of whether the prophet spoke "in the name of the LORD our God" (26:16). The elders look to precedent (26:17–19). The family of Shaphan uses its influence (26:24). The king, on the other hand, can ignore both law and precedent, as the end of Uriah shows. The same pattern recurs in chapter 36, when the officials plead with Jehoiakim not to burn the scroll and he does.

For these six chapters I read the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex word by word; Swete's printed Greek (Codex Vaticanus), which is not the critical text of Ziegler, so a Greek reading here is "Swete's Greek" unless Ziegler is named; and the transcriptions of the Dead Sea scrolls by Abegg, Bowley and Cook. The Qumran copies are 4QJer-a (4Q70), which here has only a few words of 26:10, and 4QJer-c (4Q72), which preserves parts of 26:10–13, 27:1–3 (largely restored in 27:2–3), 27:13–15, 30:6–9, 30:17–24 (from the middle of 30:17) and most of 31:1–14 and 31:19–26. Both belong to the Masoretic type; no scroll preserves 27:16–22, 29:16–20 or 30:10–15, where the Greek is much shorter or differs, and none preserves chapter 28 or 29. I read Rashi on 31:22, Radak on 31:22 and 31:31, the Targum on 30:9 and Bavli Sanhedrin 93a on Sefaria; other medieval readings named in the notes are reported by the sources listed with each note. The Greek differences in each chapter are given in the variants, and the many small omissions of titles and names ("the prophet," "king of Babylon," "the LORD of Armies," "the LORD declares") are not listed one by one: the Greek leaves out "Nebuchadnezzar" in 27:8 and 28:11, 14, "the prophet" before Jeremiah's name in chapter 28, and "the LORD declares" in many places in chapters 29 and 30.

echoes: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20; Micah 3:12; 2 Kings 23:34; Jeremiah 7:1–15; Jeremiah 36:10–26; Matthew 26:61; Acts 6:13–14

settings.to: The people of Judah's towns who came to worship in the Temple court
settings.when: At the start of Jehoiakim's reign (609/608 BC), while worshipers from Judah's towns were coming to the Temple
settings.why: To give the worshipers one more chance: if they would listen, turn back and live by the law, the LORD would change his mind. If not, the Temple would share Shiloh's fate. The words aimed to break the belief that the Temple could not fall.
settings.readers: Exiles who read the book after 586 saw the warning confirmed and learned that the disaster had been offered a way out.
views: Many scholars take this as the short report of the sermon given in full in 7:1–15.
Others think chapter 26 reports a later, shorter warning on a different feast.

settings.by: The priests and the prophets, with the people
settings.to: Jeremiah, and then the officials of Judah at the New Gate
settings.when: The same day, as soon as Jeremiah had finished speaking
settings.why: To have Jeremiah put to death under the rule that a prophet who speaks in the LORD's name what the LORD did not say must die (Deuteronomy 18:20). For the priests and prophets the sermon threatened the Temple they served; the charge of speaking "against this city" made it a matter for the king's officials.
settings.readers: Later readers see how a true word could be heard as treason and blasphemy by the people whose task was to guard the holy place.

settings.to: The officials of Judah and all the people, sitting at the New Gate
settings.when: The same day, after the priests and prophets demanded death
settings.why: To show that he spoke by the LORD's sending, not on his own; to call the court to repent; and to warn that his death would put innocent blood on the city. He does not ask for mercy; he leaves the verdict to them.
settings.readers: Later readers, exiles among them, saw a prophet who put his life in the people's hands and was proven right.

settings.to: The whole assembly at the New Gate
settings.when: After Jeremiah's defense, before the verdict was final
settings.why: To give the court a precedent: when Micah said the same under Hezekiah, the king feared the LORD and the harm was averted. The point is that a prophet's threat can be a call to repent, not treason.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book are shown that earlier prophets were part of the community's memory and that Jeremiah belongs in the same line.

settings.by: The narrator of the chapter (some read it as part of the elders' speech)
settings.to: Readers of the book, set beside the elders' appeal to Micah
settings.when: In Jehoiakim's early years; the text does not say whether before or after Jeremiah's trial
settings.why: To show that the court's verdict in Jeremiah's favor did not make every prophet safe: a king could have a prophet who said the same thing hunted down in Egypt and killed. Jeremiah lived because of Ahikam's protection (26:24).
settings.readers: Readers learn that the prophet's survival was not guaranteed by the law or by precedent, and see the king's character before chapter 36.

title: The Yoke of Babylon
sum: The LORD tells Jeremiah to make a yoke and wear it on his neck. He sends word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, whose envoys are in Jerusalem, and to Zedekiah of Judah. The message is the same: the LORD, who made the earth, has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar his servant, and any nation that will not bow its neck to Babylon will be destroyed. Those who submit will stay in their land.

Jeremiah warns against the prophets, diviners, dreamers and sorcerers who say Babylon will not rule. He also tells the priests and the people not to trust prophets who promise the quick return of the Temple vessels taken in 597: the rest will go too, until the LORD brings them back. The Greek text of this chapter is much shorter, and the Hebrew's date line (27:1) seems to have Jehoiakim's name by mistake.

views.H: The setting is 594/593 BC. Babylon's own troubles (the Chronicle reports a revolt in Nebuchadnezzar's tenth year) may have made small kingdoms hope for freedom; some historians point instead to Egypt under Psamtik II. Jeremiah's yoke is a public act against that hope. Zedekiah went to Babylon in his fourth year (51:59; the reason is not given) and revolted later anyway, which led to the siege of 588–586.
views.C: The chapter has a text problem at its start (Jehoiakim in 27:1; see the variants) and many Hebrew plusses: the Greek lacks 27:1, 27:7, the "my servant" of 27:6 and nearly all of 27:19–22. Scholars (Tov, Bogaert) usually treat these as expansions that make Jeremiah's political advice more explicit, though a minority think the Greek abridged.
views.J: Jewish readers have taken the chapter, with 29:7, as the classic case of accepting a foreign power's rule while it lasts, under God's decree. The promise that the vessels would return was kept under Cyrus (Ezra 1:7–11), which Jews and Christians both read as the fulfillment of 27:22.
views.X: The chapter has been read as a teaching on submission to civil rulers, often joined with Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2:13–17, with the caution that the same Jeremiah told people to resist a false word from a prophet.
views.F: No future event is tied to this chapter. Babylon's own fall (50–51) comes later in the book.

deep.b: Jeremiah's message is as much about God as about politics. The same God who made the earth (27:5) assigns it to whom he chooses, even a pagan king whom he calls "my servant." To resist is to resist God. The five kings Jeremiah addresses are also the five in the cup of wrath in 25:21–22, so the message is for the whole region. Chapter 28 shows how hard it was to believe.

echoes: Genesis 1; Deuteronomy 4:34; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 29:7; Jeremiah 38:2; Daniel 2:37–38; Ezra 1:7–11

settings.what: The yoke message to the five kings
settings.to: The kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, through the envoys then in Jerusalem
settings.when: About 594/593 BC, in Zedekiah's reign, when envoys from the five kingdoms had come to Jerusalem (many think to plan a revolt; the text does not say)
settings.why: To tell the rulers that Babylon rules by God's decision and that submitting is the way to stay in the land. It meant to stop a war that would end in disaster.
settings.readers: Exiles reading later learned that the disaster of 586 had been warned, and that submission had been offered.
views: The Hebrew date (Jehoiakim, 27:1) is probably a slip; the setting is Zedekiah's fourth year (28:1). The Greek lacks the verse.
The text says only that the envoys had come. A revolt plan is a historians' guess, linked to Babylon's troubles in 595/594 BC or to Egypt's new activity under Psamtik II.

settings.when: During or after the meeting with the envoys
settings.why: To urge the king to submit and so avoid the sword, famine and disease, and to warn him that the prophets of peace were speaking a lie.
settings.readers: Later readers, knowing Zedekiah's end, see that the king had a clear choice.

settings.what: The warning about the Temple vessels
settings.to: The priests and all the people
settings.when: Soon after, as prophets were promising the vessels' return
settings.why: To stop the hope of a quick return, which would encourage revolt, and to promise that the vessels would come back only when the LORD acted, not on Hananiah's timetable.
settings.readers: Readers after Cyrus saw this promise come true in Ezra 1:7–11.

title: Hananiah Breaks the Yoke
sum: In the Temple, in front of the priests and the people, the prophet Hananiah of Gibeon announces in the LORD's name that the yoke of Babylon is already broken. In two years the Temple vessels and King Jeconiah and all the exiles will be home. Jeremiah answers, "Amen! May the LORD do exactly that," but then warns that prophets of the past mostly announced war, and a prophet of peace is known only when his word comes true.

Hananiah takes the wooden yoke-bar from Jeremiah's neck and smashes it. Jeremiah goes away. Later the LORD sends him back with a new word: wood can be broken, but the nations will wear iron. Hananiah, Jeremiah says, was not sent by the LORD ("The LORD did not send you") and has taught the people a lie. He will die within the year. In the seventh month, two months later, he does.
readings: Deuteronomy 18:21–22 gives a rule: the thing happens or it does not. The chapter shows how this works in real time: two prophets say opposite things, each in the LORD's name, and only time and a further word decide.
Both men act out their message. The text lets neither sign prove anything on its own. What decides is the word that comes to Jeremiah afterward and the death that follows.

views.H: Dated to the summer of 594/593 BC. Hananiah's message of a two-year return fit the hopes of revolt that the envoys' visit in 27:3 may have stirred. Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) never returned; he lived in Babylon, and was let out of prison in 561 BC (2 Kings 25:27–30). The vessels came back only in Cyrus's reign (Ezra 1:7–11).
views.C: The Hebrew text puts the date as "that year, early in the reign, in the fourth year," and the Greek has only "the fourth year." The Greek calls Hananiah "the false prophet" and lacks several of the "the prophet" titles in this chapter. The Greek of 28:8 has only "war" where the Hebrew has "war, disaster and disease" (see the variants). The difference between "you will make iron bars" (Hebrew) and "I will make" (Greek) at 28:13 is a real variant. Many critics see in the chapter the work of the Baruch source.
views.J: Jewish readers apply the rule of Deuteronomy 18:20 here: a prophet who speaks what the LORD did not tell him must die, and Hananiah's death within two months is the Bible's own verdict. Jeremiah's polite "Amen" shows a true prophet treating an opponent first as a possible friend.
views.X: The chapter is used in Christian teaching on testing prophets, together with 1 John 4:1 and Matthew 7:15–20, and on the difference between a message people want and the message God sends.
views.F: No future event is tied to this chapter. Some futurist writers take Hananiah as a type of the false prophets of the last days (Matthew 24:24).

deep.h: How to tell a true prophet
deep.b: The Bible gives several tests. A prophet must speak in the LORD's name only (Deuteronomy 18:20) and must not lead people to other gods (13:1–5). A prediction that fails shows he was not sent (18:22). Jeremiah adds, in 28:8–9, that a prophet who foretells peace must wait to be proved. He does not say that a prophet of disaster is always right, since conditional warnings may be averted (18:7–10). The chapter shows the difficulty: neither man had proof when they spoke. What marked Jeremiah was that he waited for a word (28:12) and that his message cost him.

echoes: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22; Deuteronomy 28:48; Jeremiah 23:9–40; Ezekiel 11:13; 1 John 4:1; Matthew 7:15–20

settings.by: Hananiah son of Azzur, speaking in the LORD's name
settings.to: Jeremiah, the priests and all the people in the Temple court
settings.when: In the fifth month of Zedekiah's fourth year (594/593 BC), at a time of rumored revolt
settings.why: To reassure the people that Babylon's rule was short and to encourage resistance. The promise of the vessels and Jeconiah's return spoke to the exiles' families in Jerusalem.
settings.readers: Exiles who read Jeremiah later knew that none of this happened in two years, and that Jeremiah's letter (29) was the true word.

settings.to: Hananiah, the priests and the people
settings.why: To show that he wished the prediction true, and to state the rule by which it would be judged. He keeps the reader from supposing he is bitter.
settings.readers: Later readers learn a standard by which to judge prophets.

settings.to: Jeremiah and the crowd in the Temple court
settings.when: The same occasion, straight after Jeremiah's answer, in the fifth month of Zedekiah's fourth year (594/593 BC)
settings.why: To answer Jeremiah's sign with a bigger sign: by smashing the yoke-bar he turned Jeremiah's picture of submission into a picture of Babylon's power broken within two years, for all the nations. Jeremiah leaves without answering until the word comes (28:12).
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book see that the sign-act could be answered by a sign-act, and that only the LORD's word settled it.

settings.what: The iron yoke and the death sentence
settings.when: Some time after the bar was broken, when the word came
settings.why: To declare that Hananiah's sign had made things worse, not better, and that he would die within the year because he had spoken rebellion.
settings.readers: The reader sees the answer that was missing in the first scene.

title: A Letter to the Exiles
sum: Jeremiah writes from Jerusalem to the Judeans carried off to Babylon in 597 BC. He does not promise a quick return. He tells them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, have children and pray for the peace of the city where they live, because they will be there a long time. Only when seventy years for Babylon are over will the LORD bring them home. Meanwhile they should ignore the prophets and dreamers who say it will be soon.

The letter then names names. Ahab and Zedekiah, prophets among the exiles, will be handed to Nebuchadnezzar and burned. Shemaiah of Nehelam, who wrote to the priests in Jerusalem demanding that Jeremiah be put in the stocks, will have no descendants to see the good the LORD will do. The chapter includes the most quoted and most misused verse in the book (29:11), a promise made to a whole people about a future one generation would not see.
readings: Read as a letter to a community

The letter gives instructions for living as a minority in a foreign land, then promises return. It is the founding document of Jewish life outside the land, and Christians have drawn on it for their own sense of being exiles.
Read as part of a quarrel among prophets
Chapters 27–29 together are a debate about whether the exile will be short. Jeremiah's reply to Hananiah in Jerusalem (28) is matched by his reply to the prophets in Babylon (29).

views.H: The letter is dated after Jeconiah's deportation in 597 BC and before Zedekiah's revolt, probably in 594–593 BC. Cuneiform tablets from Al-Yahudu in Babylonia, from 572 BC onward, show Judeans farming and keeping records, so the letter's picture of settled exiles is believable. Ezekiel was one of those exiles (Ezekiel 1:1–3). The seventy years of 29:10 end either at Cyrus's decree (538 BC) or at the Temple's rebuilding (516 BC).
views.C: The Greek lacks 29:14 (mostly), 29:16–20, and the words "a future, and hope with it" in 29:11, and has "land" for "city" in 29:7 (see the variants). Critics debate whether the long Hebrew additions are later; some see 29:16–20 as an addition meant to blame the people still in Jerusalem. Critics differ on how much of the letter goes back to Jeremiah: the commentaries of Holladay and Lundbom treat its core as his, while Carroll sees heavy Deuteronomistic editing. The names of Ahab, Zedekiah and Shemaiah are otherwise unknown.
views.J: The letter is treated in Jewish tradition as the basis for life in the Diaspora: pray for the welfare of the place where one lives (compare Mishnah Avot 3:2, which urges prayer for the government). The seventy years are linked with Daniel 9; see the topic page for the different counts.
views.X: Augustine took 29:7 to mean that Christians, like the exiles, may use the peace of the earthly city (City of God 19.26). 1 Peter calls Christians "exiles" (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11). Verse 11 has become one of the most quoted promises in popular Christianity; scholars warn that it was written to the whole exile community.
views.F: Futurist writers connect the seventy years with the seventy weeks of Daniel 9 and treat the return as a pattern for a final gathering of Israel (29:14), but most readings place 29:10–14 in the return under Cyrus.

deep.b: The verse is addressed to the whole exile community in the plural, after the seventy years are over (29:10). The instruction around it asks them to settle down, pray for Babylon and wait. Many Christians apply it to the individual, often as a promise of success or of a plan for one's life. Careful teachers hold that the verse shows God's character toward his people and that the New Testament extends such promises to those who are in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), but that it does not guarantee a given outcome to a given person. Many of the adults taken in 597 BC would not live to see the return that 29:10 puts seventy years away. The Greek omits "a future, and hope with it" (see the variant), which shows the phrase was not always remembered.

The exiles did not live in a prison camp. Tablets from villages such as Al-Yahudu ("Judah-town") show Judeans holding land, paying taxes and writing contracts. Ezekiel's "elders" came to his house to hear him (Ezekiel 8:1; 14:1). Jeremiah's instruction to "build and plant" described what many already did, but it stood against the opinion that the stay was brief.

echoes: Deuteronomy 4:29–30; Deuteronomy 28:30; Jeremiah 1:10; Jeremiah 24:1–10; Jeremiah 25:11–12; Daniel 9:2; 2 Chronicles 36:21; 1 Peter 2:11

settings.by: Jeremiah, writing in the LORD's name
settings.to: The elders, priests, prophets and all the people carried to Babylon with Jeconiah in 597 BC
settings.when: A few years after the deportation, in Zedekiah's reign, carried by Elasah and Gemariah on Zedekiah's embassy to Nebuchadnezzar
settings.why: To tell the exiles to settle, because the stay would last about seventy years; to say the LORD had not forgotten them; and to stop the prophets among them whose promises of a quick return would unsettle them and lead to revolt.
settings.readers: Exiles and their children reading the whole book found an explanation of why they were there and a promise (29:10–14) that they would come home.
views: Counted from 605 BC (the first year of Nebuchadnezzar) to Cyrus (538), or from 586 to 516.

settings.to: The exiles, and Shemaiah of Nehelam by name
settings.when: After Zephaniah the priest read Shemaiah's letter to Jeremiah
settings.why: To expose Shemaiah as a man who spoke without being sent and who tried to have a prophet silenced, and to declare that he would have no descendants.
settings.readers: The reader sees that opposition to Jeremiah came from inside the exile community too.

title: The Book of Consolation Opens
sum: After the letter, the book turns to a poem of rescue. The LORD tells Jeremiah to write the words down: days are coming when he will turn the fortunes of his people, Israel and Judah, and bring them back to the land he gave their ancestors. The first poem opens with terror, with strong men clutching their hips like women in labor, and then calls it "a season of anguish for Jacob," out of which he will be saved.

The LORD will break the yoke from their neck and raise up David their king. Jacob should not be afraid: the nations will be finished off, but Israel will be disciplined, not destroyed. Their wound is past healing, and the LORD himself caused it for their guilt. Yet he will make new skin grow, rebuild the city on its mound, give a ruler from their own number and make them his people again. The chapter closes on the storm of the LORD's anger, which will not turn back until it has done its work.

views.H: The poems speak to "Israel and Judah" (30:3-4). Many scholars hold that the oldest of them were meant for the north in Josiah's day, about 627–609 BC, when Jeremiah hoped for the northern tribes' return; the headings and a few verses address Judah after 597 or 586. The fulfillment of the promise began with the return under Cyrus in 538 BC, which restored only part of what is described (a king from David's line did not return to rule).
views.C: The chapter is poetry with prose headings (30:1–4). The Greek lacks 30:10–11 (which it has in the oracle on Egypt), 30:15 and 30:22. The Qumran copy 4QJer-c preserves parts of 30:6–9 and 30:17–24 and agrees with the Hebrew apart from spelling and small readings; of 30:17 it has only the second half. Verses 8–9 are prose and are often seen as an editor's addition, since they speak of a king where the poem speaks of a nation.
views.J: The Targum of the Prophets reads 30:9 as "Messiah the son of David" (the Aramaic text, read on Sefaria). The Book of Consolation (30–31) is read by Jews as a central expression of hope for return, and 31:2–20 is the haftarah on the second day of Rosh Hashanah.
views.X: Christians read 30:9 and 30:21 as pointing to Jesus the Son of David (Luke 1:32–33), and 30:17's healing with the healing of Israel and of the nations through him. The older English name for 30:7, "Jacob's trouble," has been linked with the tribulation of Matthew 24:21 and Revelation 7:14.
views.F: Dispensational and premillennial readers see 30:7–9 as a future time of tribulation for Israel followed by the reign of David's heir in the millennial kingdom (Walvoord; Pentecost). Amillennial readers see the promises met in Christ and the church, and Jewish readers in the age of the Messiah.

deep.b: The command to write (30:2) turns the following poems into a sealed hope for readers who would have the book after the destruction. It is the center of the Jeremiah that most readers cherish. It follows directly after the letter's "seventy years" and opens with promises that reverse the earlier verbs of the commission: to "pull up and pull down" now gives way to "build and plant" (31:28).

echoes: Isaiah 35; Hosea 3:5; Ezekiel 34:23–24; Jeremiah 8:22; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Jeremiah 28:2; Jeremiah 46:27–28; Matthew 24:21

settings.what: The oracles of rescue for Israel and Judah
settings.by: The LORD through Jeremiah, who is told to write them in a book
settings.to: The people of Israel and Judah, first the northern tribes and later the exiles of Judah
settings.when: Undated. Many scholars place the earliest poems in Josiah's reign and the framework after 586
settings.why: To give the shattered people a reason to hope: their wound is deserved but not final, and their rescue will come from the LORD himself. The poems say that discipline is not rejection.
settings.readers: After 586, exiles in Babylon, in Egypt and in Judah read these as the answer to the question whether the LORD was finished with them.
views: The core poems come from Jeremiah in Josiah's day, addressed to the north (Bright; Thompson; Holladay).
The poems were composed or reshaped after the fall of Jerusalem (Carroll).

title: Rachel Weeps; a New Covenant
sum: The Book of Consolation moves to the north and the whole people. The LORD loves Israel with a love that lasts forever and will build her up again. The exiles will return weeping and praying, led by a father to streams of water. Rachel weeps in Ramah for her lost children, but the LORD says to stop weeping: they will come back. Ephraim confesses, "Turn me back, and I will turn back," and the LORD, whose insides churn, says, "I will surely have mercy on him." A new thing in the land: a woman will surround a man.

Then Jeremiah wakes from a sweet sleep, and the LORD promises to watch over his people to build and to plant as he once watched to uproot. No one will say that the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth went numb. Days are coming when the LORD will cut a new covenant with the houses of Israel and Judah, not like the one they broke. He will write his law on their hearts, all will know him, and he will forgive and no longer remember their sin. Israel's future is as firm as the sun and moon. The chapter ends with a rebuilt Jerusalem, holy to the LORD, never again to be uprooted.
readings: The chapter speaks first to the north (Ephraim, Samaria, Rachel) and then to Judah. The new covenant is promised to "the house of Israel and the house of Judah" as one people.

Matthew uses 31:15 for Bethlehem (Matthew 2:17–18). Luke, Paul and Hebrews use 31:31–34 for the covenant sealed in Christ's blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; Hebrews 8:8–12; 10:16–17), the longest Old Testament quotation in the New.

views.H: The Ephraim poems (31:2–22) most likely belong to Josiah's time, when Jeremiah hoped for the northern tribes; the final form speaks to the exiles of 586. Ramah (31:15) was a gathering point for captives in 586 BC (40:1). The rebuilt city (31:38–40) began to come true under Nehemiah in 445 BC (Nehemiah 3; 12:39), but "never again" cannot be met by the history of Jerusalem, which was destroyed in AD 70 and again in AD 135.
views.C: The chapter is a collection of poems with prose links (31:23–30, 38–40). The Greek differs in 31:2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 19, 22, 32 and 33, and the Qumran copy 4QJer-c preserves most of 31:1–14 and 31:19–26. It agrees with the Hebrew apart from spelling and four small readings (31:8, 31:9, 31:12 and a stray letter in 31:22), two of which the Greek shares (see the variants). The Greek also differs in 31:34. The "new covenant" passage (31:31–34) is often assigned to a Deuteronomic editor, but others hold it for Jeremiah, since it fits his early criticism of the heart (17:1).
views.J: Rashi reads 31:22 as the woman (Israel) going after the man (God), and Radak reads the new covenant as the same Torah, now kept: he cites Malachi 3:22 (Hebrew numbering; 4:4 in English) and says there will never be a new Torah apart from the one given at Sinai (as read on Sefaria). The haftarah for the second day of Rosh Hashanah is 31:2–20, paired with the binding of Isaac, and it includes Rachel's weeping.
views.X: Matthew sees Rachel's weeping in the killing of the children at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18). The Last Supper cup is "the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and Hebrews 8 and 10 quote 31:31–34 to say that Christ's sacrifice makes the old covenant obsolete (Hebrews 8:13) and that sins are forgiven for good. Early Christian writers read 31:22 of Mary.
views.F: Dispensationalists expect the new covenant to be fulfilled with Israel in the age to come, and the rebuilt Jerusalem of 31:38–40 in the millennium. Other premillennialists and amillennialists hold that the covenant is now in force in the church, and that its fullness comes with the new creation. Jewish hope places the whole chapter in the days of the Messiah.

deep.h: The new covenant in the Old Testament and the New
deep.b: Jeremiah's words are the only place in the Old Testament that speak of a "new covenant." He lists what is new: the law is placed inside, everyone knows the LORD, sin is forgiven. What is not new is the law itself and the formula "I will be their God, and they will be my people." Ezekiel (36:26–27) and Deuteronomy (30:6) speak of the same inner change. The Qumran community called itself the "new covenant" (Damascus Document CD VI, 19). In the New Testament, Jesus names the cup "the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20, with 1 Corinthians 11:25), Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6), and Hebrews quotes the whole passage twice (8:8–12; 10:16–17). The Jewish reading, as Radak gives it, is that the Torah does not change: what is new is that Israel will keep it. Christian readings differ on whether the covenant replaces, renews or fulfills the covenant with Israel (see the cards below).
deep.refs: Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Deuteronomy 30:6; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Hebrews 8:8–13; Hebrews 10:16–17

deep.b: First, the poem imagines the mother of the northern tribes weeping as her children go into captivity past Ramah. Second, it is a promise that she will be comforted (31:16–17). Third, Matthew links it with Bethlehem, where Rachel's tomb stood in tradition, and the children Herod killed (Matthew 2:16–18). Matthew's wording is close to the Greek Jeremiah but is his own. Whether Matthew means that Jeremiah foretold the killing, or that Israel's exile story is happening again (typology), is debated; the context in Jeremiah, with its immediate promise of return, suggests that Matthew expects the same ending.

echoes: Genesis 35:16–20; Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1–8; Isaiah 54:8; Ezekiel 18:2–4; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Matthew 2:17–18; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Hebrews 8:8–13; Hebrews 10:16–17

settings.by: The LORD through Jeremiah, with Ephraim's confession quoted
settings.to: The northern tribes (Ephraim, Samaria) and, in the finished book, all Israel in exile
settings.when: Undated. Many scholars place them in Josiah's reign (627–609 BC), when northern territory came under his rule; the book's readers received them after 586
settings.why: To promise that the LORD's love for the north, destroyed in 722/721 BC, had not ended, that he would bring the scattered back and that his anger had not cancelled his fatherhood. It aimed to make people who felt rejected able to hope.
settings.readers: Exiles from Judah, after 586, learned that the promise given to the north also covered them.
views: Written for the north under Josiah (Bright; Holladay).
Reworked or composed in the exile (Carroll).

settings.what: Judah blessed; the end of the sour-grapes proverb
settings.to: The people of Judah and Israel, who blamed their fathers for the disaster
settings.when: Undated; the proverb was in use before and after 586
settings.why: To declare that the LORD would build as he had torn down, and that each person would answer for his own guilt, so that no one could say that the exile was only the fault of ancestors.
settings.readers: Exiles who used the proverb to excuse themselves were told that the time of waiting was ending.

settings.to: The house of Israel and the house of Judah, the whole people
settings.when: Undated; "days are coming," after the fall of Jerusalem in most readings
settings.why: To promise that the covenant the people broke at Sinai would not be the last word: the LORD would give them a new heart and forgive them, and all would know him. It answers the question of what could be done about a people that could not keep its law.
settings.readers: Exiles in 586 learned that the broken covenant did not end God's relationship. Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8), and Jews as promise of a Torah finally kept.
views: The Torah stays; the newness is that Israel will keep it.
A new covenant in Christ's blood, with different views on Israel's place.
The community called itself the "new covenant" (CD VI, 19).

settings.what: The permanence of Israel and the rebuilt city
settings.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem
settings.when: Undated; after the fall of Jerusalem in most readings
settings.why: To say that Israel's existence was as certain as the sun and moon, and to describe the boundaries of the city that would be rebuilt as holy to the LORD, including the places of death and ashes.
settings.readers: Exiles who feared that Israel was finished.

traditions.q: Who is the "new covenant" of Jeremiah 31:31–34 made with, and does it replace the covenant with Israel?
views: The new covenant is established by Christ's blood and the church is its people, but the Old Covenant "has never been revoked" and the Jewish people remain beloved for the gifts that are irrevocable (Catechism 121, 839; the New Law is a law of grace, 1966).

The new covenant is fulfilled in Christ and lived in the church. The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom has the words over the cup, "this is my blood of the new covenant," and chrismation after baptism seals the believer with the Spirit who writes the law on the heart (Ware, The Orthodox Church, on the sacraments).

The new covenant is the Gospel promise of forgiveness (31:34) given for Christ's sake and received by faith. The Law still accuses until the Spirit writes it on the heart, and the regenerate then delight in it (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration V and VI).

There is one covenant of grace in two administrations: promised under the law, fully shown in the gospel. The new covenant is therefore the same covenant in a new form, made with the one people of God, Jew and Gentile (Westminster Confession 7.5–6; Calvin, Institutes 2.10–11).

The new covenant is the gospel form of the covenant of grace, and everyone in it knows the LORD and has forgiveness. It is the covenant of believers, whose sign is believer's baptism (31:34; Second London Confession ch. 7 on God's covenant and ch. 29 on baptism).

The promise names the house of Israel and the house of Judah and will be fulfilled with national Israel in the kingdom age. The church shares in its spiritual blessings now through Christ's blood (Luke 22:20) without replacing Israel (Walvoord; Pentecost).

The covenant is made with the Jewish people, and Yeshua inaugurated it. It does not abolish the Torah: the law written on the heart gives the power to keep it. Gentile believers join through Messiah (Stern, Jewish New Testament Commentary on Hebrews 8; Kinzer).

traditions.q: Does "they will all know me" (31:34) limit the new covenant community to believers, and so rule out baptizing infants?
views: Yes. In the new covenant every member knows the LORD, so only those who profess repentance and faith are proper subjects of baptism (Second London Confession 29.2).

Yes. The church is a gathered community of those who have repented and chosen to follow Christ, and baptism follows faith, not birth (Schleitheim Confession, art. 1; Mennonite Confession of Faith, 1995).

No. The covenant of grace includes believers and their children, as Acts 2:39 says. Baptism, like circumcision, is given to the children of believing parents, and "they will all know me" (31:34) is the goal of the covenant, not a test applied at the font (Westminster Confession 28.4; Calvin, Institutes 4.16).

No. Baptism is God's act, which gives faith, and infants are to be baptized because God's promise is for them. Knowing the LORD (31:34) is what God works through the Word and baptism, not a condition set on the font (Luther, Large Catechism, on baptism).

No. "They will all know me" names the gift of the new covenant, which God gives by grace; it is not a test applied before baptism. Baptism gives new birth, and children also need it. The church baptizes infants in the faith of the church, as it has from early times (Catechism 1250, 1253).

No. Infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion together, in the faith of the church; the knowing of 31:34 is the life of the whole people of God into which the child is brought, not an entry requirement (Ware, The Orthodox Church, on baptism and chrismation).
No. "The baptism of young children is in any wise to be retained in the Church, as most agreeable with the institution of Christ" (Thirty-Nine Articles, art. 27).
No. "The baptism of young children is to be retained in the Church" (Articles of Religion of the Methodist Episcopal Church, art. 17, from Wesley).
